en: Preface to the Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Avalokiteśvara Chapter.
Generally speaking, the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*) is the primary standard for the propagation section of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Because Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara has a karmic affinity with the sentient beings of this land, he adapts to their capacities through the medium of sound; there is no suffering from which he does not deliver them, and no suffering that he does not extract.

Because he saves [beings], he is called Guanyin (Avalokiteśvara). How sublime is what is known as the "Universal Gate" (*Pumen*), wherein one swiftly realizes *samādhi* through the conditions of karmic capacity.

During the Sui dynasty, the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai composed two fascicles of the *Bie xing Guanyin xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Separate Practice of Avalokiteśvara) to explain the treatise, and two fascicles of the *Jie yi shu* (Commentary on the Exegesis) to explain the sūtra;
these were circulated separately from the main body of his works. Later, during the Song dynasty, there was the Venerable Zongyi of Siming.

The *Record of the Profound Meaning of Guanyin* (Guanyin xuanyi ji) in four fascicles and the *Commentary on the Record* (Shuji) in four fascicles each formed separate volumes and were kept in the Tripitaka;

thus, they were inconvenient for beginners to consult. Layman Wang Jichang of the Ministry of Works wished to reunite these two parts of the "Holy Practice" (shengxing), and having begun the draft in the first year of the Wuchen era of the Chongzhen reign, he was about to complete it when his disciple Faji received a request from Jinling to include them in the Tripitaka.
Yin-yuan brought the manuscript to visit the Layman, who immediately acted as its witness and sponsor, first donating thirty taels of his stipend to carve the blocks for circulation.
In the autumn of the Jisi year, when the venerable elder Min Zhao-yu of Wu-xing passed by the hermitage and spoke of it, he too generously offered his assistance;
furthermore, the Layman Chu-xian supplemented the funds. This may truly be called the flowing of the Buddha-dharma.
This penetration was not accidental. Should there be those hereafter who read these teachings, they will immediately awaken to the samādhi of their own nature.

When mind after mind and mental state after mental state mutually verify one another, how could this sutra and its commentaries—containing inexhaustible profound meanings—be seen without the joyful assistance of lay devotees? How else could it be so?
Written by Bohui of Pútí Ān, with respectful greetings.
Regarding the supplementary remarks appended to the combined edition of the *Commentary on the Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara*:
A close friend urged me, saying, "I have heard that the *Commentary on the Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara* skillfully employs the principle of the inherent nature."
It penetrates the hidden and manifests the responsive resonance; it reveals non-action and provides deliverance. Students should most earnestly investigate this.

However, as the various sections circulate separately, they are inconvenient for beginners to read. In the past, Yuxi once attempted to compile them into a unified collection, but I regret that his compilation was not correct and instead threw the internal structure into disarray.
Although former masters have provided detailed evaluations and reached definitive conclusions, the text remains as it was.
[The text] was moved. It might be called "Correcting the Suspended Compilation. Why do you, Master, not strive to add critical collation to satisfy the inquiries of the young and ignorant?
I firmly declined, yet could not avoid it; thus this undertaking was made. Furthermore, I told him: "For a master of practice is the hope of the age.
Once the division of the compilation was complete, one person would proofread it while another would cross-check it, alternating with one another.

If realization were immediately followed by practice, then the principle would surely remain intact. However, as seen in the *Xuánwén* (second volume of the *Huìběn*), within the section on "Object and Wisdom" (*míngjìngzhì*), it refutes [the opponent] from the standpoint of principle;
this entire section is explained together with its commentary, which further cites the *Mādhyamaka-śāstra* to refute it.

In the *Ke-yü* (Sectional Phrases), thirty-four characters are missing, rendering the text unreadable; consequently, the two sections of the *Zǐkē* (Sub-sections) are left floating without affiliation.

Furthermore, in the *Yìshū* (Commentary on the Meaning), Volume Three of the *Huìběn* (Combined Edition), Zhàn’ān’s private commentary appends the three characters “jié wén mò zhù” (at the end of the concluding text, he records) before the two characters “jié tàn” (concluding praise).

This appears to be a continuation of the record from the *Shūsù*, yet the omissions and excesses are all too evident. Nevertheless, such negligent errors have been preserved; therefore, I venture to say that what is currently...
The current edition of the *Xinghui* must certainly not be its complete original. I suspect it was obtained by a bookseller in a rural village from some scattered fragments and disordered folios;
it has not been corrected, but merely patched together and rushed into print. Most of the extreme errors stem from this very source.
Now, your exhortation is indeed appropriate. I shall exert my humble efforts to collate and edit it, restoring it to its completeness.
Thus, the achievements of former masters shall likewise remain imperishable forever.

The *Catalogue of Tiantai Teachings and Contemplations by Ciyun* states: "The *Mysterious Meaning of Avalokiteśvara* in two fascicles; the *Commentary on the Meaning of Avalokiteśvara* in two fascicles.
The number of fascicles for the *Mysterious Commentary* in the Qing edition is the same.

The *Kaigen Zenkō Ki-shu Jitsuroku* (Record of the Master’s True Biography by Zenkō of the Kaiyuan Era) states: "The *Guan-yin Xuan Shu Ji* (Commentary on the Profound [Commentary] on Avalokiteśvara) consists of four volumes in total;
the Qingzang contains four volumes of the *Xuanji* and four volumes of the *Shuji*, and the Mingzang is the same.

Although the length of the text in the current edition varies, when the volumes are adjusted accordingly, the *Ji* (Commentary) comprises four volumes each for the *Xuan* (Profound Commentary) and the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) that it explains.
Regarding the convention for distinguishing sections: raise one character to indicate the subject (*neng*) and lower one character to indicate the object (*suo*).

When explaining the title, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) is raised by one character and the *Ji* (Commentary) is lowered by one character. When explaining the main text, the *Sūtra* text and the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) are both lowered by one character.
The headings of the *Ji* are marked with a circle (○), and the explanations of the *Ji* are marked with 【記】, in order to distinguish them from the *Shu*.

Regarding characters, one should select those that are authentic over those that are vulgar or spurious, yet one must not be exhaustive. Within the text, the characters "bian" (辯) and "bian" (辨) are used interchangeably;
for the sake of consistency, they shall follow a single convention here. Those who read this may extract the meaning according to the flow of the text.
Regarding the principles of collation and editing: both the *Xuanshu* (Profound Commentary) and the *Ji* (Record) take the Qing edition as their primary basis and are compared against other editions.
If another edition is correct while the Qing edition contains an error beyond doubt, it is directly adopted in place of the latter.
If the wording differs between editions yet each carries a valid meaning, the superior version is adopted; the inferior version is recorded above the grid-line. Furthermore, or...
Regarding citations: if there is any ambiguity concerning the source text, one should consult the original location to verify and correct it.

Furthermore, where passages from other locations are used as equivalents—such as supplying missing characters or completing sentences—all such instances are marked at the top of the grid for others to accept or reject as they see fit.
Although this may invite criticism for acting arbitrarily, it is also motivated by the desire to facilitate easier reading.

I have extracted the topical outline (ke-wen) and appended it to this work. I have arranged it as a single continuous progression; where the text is extensive, I have provided pointers to the ultimate destination.
My intention is merely to facilitate easy investigation and inquiry.

Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha has spoken of it by various names.
Now, ten principles are employed to explain the Middle Way in brief: (1) person and dharma; (2) compassion; (3) merit and wisdom; (4) true and responsive bodies; (5) medicine and jewels;
(6) the hidden and the manifest; (7) the provisional and the real; (8) the fundamental and the trace; (9) the conditions and the fulfillment; and (10) knowledge and cessation.
These ten principles are arranged in sequence according to two meanings: contemplation and teaching.

Regarding the contemplation of persons and dharmas as the primary focus: the reason persons are treated first and dharmas second is that one must first clarify compassion and loving-kindness (karuṇā-maitrī).
[Entrustment] The three non-differentiated types of compassion and loving-kindness—the sequence of compassion followed by loving-kindness—each possess two meanings.
3. The Meaning of Cultivating Merit First and Wisdom Later (with the True and Responsive [Buddhas] as the Fourth);
5. The Sequence of Medicine and Jewels (with the True and Responsive [Buddhas] as the Fifth).

The three delusions are named "grasping at marks" (taking the sixth position, with a sub-note); "the hidden and the manifest" have no sequence before or after (taking the seventh position, including both);
and "the provisional and the real" have a sequence of before and after—these are the three meanings.
The Original and the Traced (Honjaku) occupy the eighth [section] (including both);

the sequence of the Original and the Traced regarding the Conditions and the Response (Enryō) occupies the ninth (including both); the Conditions and the Response in relation to nature, virtue, wisdom, and severance occupy the tenth;
and the sequential order as clarified through the various teachings follows below.
Across the four teachings, there are ten pairs each;

these are established by clarifying that the title of the *Avataṃsaka* possesses six meanings (and why that sūtra lacks four meanings— namely, the provisional and the real, the original and the trace,
conditions and fulfillment, and wisdom and severance).

Chapter on the Supernatural Powers: Entrustment Limited to the Meaning of Original Transformation (The Record states: "The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattvas who had emerged from the earth and those who had emerged from the earth to transmit the sutra").
The Tripitaka clarifies that the person and the Dharma consist of compassion and wisdom, with nothing remaining;
the three Tripitakas are named after the teachings and meanings of the Two Vehicles.
The Great Master sets forth objections to clarify that while the Tripiṭaka possesses only three meanings,
the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā also possesses six meanings yet lacks four; furthermore,
these six meanings also differ between the ancient and the present.
Regarding the six layers of original and trace: prior to this, there were only four [aspects] lacking two;
now, with the entry into extinction and *nirvāṇa* of the Lamp-Light Kāśyapa in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the ten meanings are fully complete for both the sharp and dull faculties (along with the others).

The Ten Dharmas Encompass All (Postscript): A brief summary involves comparative evaluation;
based on the six meanings and five flavors, the ten dharmas are explained in detail below.

First, it clarifies persons and dharmas (Postscript): the provisional names and real dharmas, the characteristics of the five aggregates, and the constant [truth] of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. (Postscript).
The contemplation of impermanence differs from that of Avalokiteśvara’s Universal Gate; these respectively pertain to persons and dharmas.
Persons and dharmas encompass both ordinary beings and sages. (Entrustment: Transforming the five aggregates into the five elements.
Regarding the statement that "sentient beings are the unsurpassed Buddhas," this refers to ordinary persons and those of the six paths of human and heavenly existence.

According to the meaning of the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and the four gates, it clarifies that within the gate of "existence" regarding persons and dharmas, there is no absence of dharma; yet, because one contemplates the preceding and succeeding moments, it is provisionally said to be "non-existent."
The *Tattvasiddhi*’s three types of provisional designation differ from those of the Mahāyāna;
the gate of "both" and the gate of "neither" (attached). The terminology resembles that of the Middle Way, yet the principle resides solely within the essence of emptiness.
Emptiness pervades the three teachings. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the nature of form is like the nature of the self, and so forth.
Contemplating the emptiness of persons is the seed of the clarifying cause;
the two emptinesses of person and phenomena, and the two emptinesses of nature and characteristics, are actually contemplated simultaneously.
Contemplating the emptiness of phenomena is the seed of the supporting cause.
Through the detailed and exhaustive differentiation of the various types of relative seeds,
one clarifies that the Buddha-nature is neither identical to nor separate from the six dharmas;
by correlating quiescence and illumination with the provisional and the real, one elucidates the stages of partial realization according to the three Buddha-natures.

the Distinctions in the Sequence of Cause and Effect Regarding the Removal of Suffering and the Bestowal of Happiness.
The four great vows are all for the sake of others, or alternatively, three [vows] pertain to one's own practice.
Based on the objects of the Four Noble Truths, the four great vows are generated; these differ according to the four teachings.
Extinction is not the ultimate truth; rather, it is through the extinction of causes that one realizes the truth. The distinct principles follow conditions.
The four kinds of Four Noble Truths in the Separate Teaching (biejiao) are all termed "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*);

whether they are contrary, compliant, or both non-contrary and non-compliant, they all rely upon the dharmadhātu’s perfect interfusion and the three types of compassion— compassion for sentient beings, etc.

the Sage desires to make this known so that even insects may understand the benefits of the Sage.

these are collectively and briefly judged in four propositions regarding the relative heights of the fundamental and ultimate.
There are nine explanations of the conditions and causes (pratyaya-hetu), including the acquisition of names and the differences in the conditions and causes across the four teachings.

The Innate Virtues of the Conditions for Enlightenment and the Causes for Enlightenment (Postscript): Citing the Text on the Innate Conditions for Enlightenment and the Causes for Enlightenment—All phenomena are by their very nature originally empty; this is the innate cause for enlightenment.
Sentient beings possess the first dhyāna and the cessation-attainment; these are the determinate natures that serve as the causal conditions for enlightenment.

Relying on the nature (xing), conditions (yuan), and understanding (liao) to accomplish the characteristics of cultivated virtue (xiu-de): this section does not discuss the six stages of identity (*liu-ji*), but rather provides ten explanations to clarify the general characteristics of the two virtues of wisdom (*zhi*) and severance (*duan*).

Regarding the names and meanings of "perfect purity" (*yuan-jing*) and "purity through skillful means" (*fang-bian-jing*), the distinctions between the virtues of severance in the Mahayana and Hinayana vehicles are as follows.
In the Mahāyāna, the virtue of severance reaches the realization that evil is identical to the nature of evil;
when hidden, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*, and when manifest, it is called the *dharmakāya*.
The great sutras distinguish between cause and effect regarding Buddha-nature based on the cultivation and the nature [of phenomena].
The three causes and three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal; this Mahāyāna principle is common to all sūtras.
This chapter contains ten meanings. Fourth, the "Discrimination" section below concerns the Universal Gate Dharma Prince’s response to the present discrimination.
The fourfold analysis of the relationship between persons and dharmas proceeds through the five flavors to clarify this Vaipulya scripture;
the Universal Gate chapter alternately presents persons and dharmas,
and names such as Śāriputra and other disciples are cited in terms of a single dharma-gate.
The reason why only the two gates of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are discussed here, while joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are not,
is that King Aśoka was to die after seven days;
because the factors of dhyāna proceed from joy first and then to bliss (*sukha*), whereas the four immeasurables proceed from bliss first and then to joy.
Regarding the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), this distinguishes them from the contemplations practiced by non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles;
it clarifies how Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom extracts beings from suffering and his universal gate bestows blessings and joy.
Thus, blessings and wisdom are presented in a tetralemma (*catuṣkoṭi*), which is elucidated through the analogy of the five flavors (*pañcarasa*).
Now, in this Great Sūtra, merit and wisdom are mutually complete; the Buddha-nature has five names;
the true and the responsive are distinguished through four propositions;
the two benefits of permanence and intermission are inseparable; and there is the analogy of the two birds flying together. (Entrustment)
The Hīnayāna *tathatā* and *nirmāṇakāya* each possess the meanings of permanence and interruption; the Mahāyāna *tathatā* and *nirmāṇakāya* each possess the meanings of permanence and interruption.
The medicinal herb and the jewel each provide the dual benefits of extracting suffering and bestowing joy through both hidden and manifest means; thus, there are thirty-six propositions in total.

Regarding the two wisdoms of provisional and real and the liberation from the two sufferings of provisional and real, the fourfold analysis (*catuskoṭi*) generally distinguishes between the original and the manifested; in each case, there is both the extraction of suffering and the bestowal of bliss.
In the preceding question-and-answer, the manifested follows the original; in the subsequent question-and-answer, the original follows the manifested.

The True and the Responsive are horizontally categorized according to the single lifetime of the origin and the trace; the Origin and the Trace of Avalokiteśvara are vertically categorized according to the three periods of time.

Regarding essence and function, antiquity and modernity, and the nature of both good and evil—[this is] the entrustment of the record. As for the nature of evil, it is that which is discussed by our own school.
The Buddha does not sever the inherent evil of icchantikas, nor does he sever the inherent good of icchantikas;
"icchantika" is translated as "one who lacks desire," and is also translated as "one who lacks faith.
The terms "inherent good" and "inherent evil" signify a gateway to the Dharma.
This clarifies that while the Buddha initiates the cultivation of goodness, he does not initiate the cultivation of evil;

therefore, it raises the meaning of the *ālaya-vijñāna* being perfumed by the person of the stages (*bhūmi*) to address the difficulty regarding the non-interruption of innate evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*) and the non-permanence of cultivated evil (*abhyāsa-pāpa*), which generally subsumes the views of annihilationism and eternalism. Furthermore, it establishes the wisdom that uproots suffering and bestows bliss as the antidote.

This is because there are two senses to the names of the four natures: "natural" (*tianran*), "relative" (*xiangdai*), and "absolute" (*juedai*). Regarding the absolute, there are two interpretations.
By refuting the four types of self-nature and adhering to one view, one becomes possessed of the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), losing the Four Truths, the Three Jewels,
the three kinds of selfhood of ordinary persons, and the single self of the Arhat.
Ordinary beings cling to the principle that the inconceivable realm of object and wisdom is like the characters carved by insects gnawing through wood;

this is explained through the fourfold formulation (catuṣkoṭi) based on the four *siddhāntas* (the four conditions), using the analogy of a golden probe removing a cataract from the eye to represent the inconceivable realm of object and wisdom.
The inconceivable realm and wisdom are characterized by the mark of emptiness; their nature is inconceivable and their marks are empty.
To analyze this, Nāgārjuna first refuted attachments in his commentaries on the sūtras; we shall now follow that same precedent.

The three kinds of worlds, the world of dharmas, the dharma-realm, names and meanings, the hundred realms and thousand dharmas, and the numerical categories of dharmas.
Now it is clarified that the thousand dharmas are themselves the three thousand [realms]. Regarding the two objects—self and other—they are divided according to the three dharmas.
The two objects—internal and external—and the mind are the proximate essentials to be refuted;
solitary form (*rūpa*) is not complete, for it lacks the thirty thousand myriad dharmas. Form alone is spoken of in the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*), wherein form is created by the mind;
its entire substance is mind, and form is likewise so.
The various texts focus exclusively on the mind because it is easier to manifest the difficult;
observing the true reality of the body and observing the Buddha are likewise so. These three dharmas are without difference (hereafter follows the non-difference of the three truths).
This concludes the commentary on the text regarding the non-difference of the three [truths] (entrusted to the two modes of creation: phenomena and principle).

[Commentary on the Pronunciation of "Shi" (Releasing), appended as a note: The Buddha is not merely the ultimate fruit; rather, he refers specifically to those of perfect capacity (*pariniṣpanna-yogya*).
Because the Bodhisattva observes the capacities of the three karmas [of sentient beings], he is titled only "Guanyin" (Avalokiteśvara).
Regarding the six meanings proposed by ancient masters, this school refutes their partial interpretations and explains [the name] through the perfect completeness of the three karmas.
The third fascicle: Part Two, Explaining the Contemplation of the Lower [Realms], wherein even mental karma possesses the three types of action.
The six objects of the realm of Avalokiteśvara are concluded as: (dependent origination, the four truths, the three truths, the two truths, the one truth, and the truthless).
Since the ten suchnesses share the same nature as dependent origination, they are not established separately.
There are five sequences of clear-contemplative wisdom: (four for dependent origination, four for the four truths, two for the three truths, seven for the two truths, and one for the one truth).
The object is that which accords with the contemplation of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the reliance on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, there are two meanings—general and particular—concerning its fourfold negation (*catuṣkoṭi*). (Note) The general [contemplation] is sudden observation; the particular is gradual observation.

The characteristics of the three successive contemplations are as follows: (Note) In the third [stage], the Middle Way, all three contemplations are employed together; it is named "Middle" based on its predominance.
The three wisdoms are defined as follows:

the wisdom of contemplating names and meanings is called the wisdom that contemplates causes and effects in their distinction; the wisdom of contemplating causes is the [wisdom of] the four vehicles; and the wisdom of contemplating effects is the Great Sūtra.
The four contemplations of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* correspond to the three contemplations of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-vaipulya-sūtra-mañjūṣā*;

this clarification of their opening and closing corresponds to the opening and closing of the three sūtras. Furthermore, the three contemplations correspond to the five eyes, and the three contemplations correspond to the four teachings; additionally, the four contemplations of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* correspond to the four teachings.
Regarding the three contemplations in relation to the four teachings,
there are instances where a single Buddha expounds the four teachings, and instances where four Buddhas mutually expound the four teachings;
because there are four Buddhas, there are four sites for their respective assistants.
Although it is inexpressible, it can also be explained by way of causes and conditions:
the characteristics of the Bodhisattva of the Three Piṭakas at the initial arousal of the mind who fulfills the six perfections—
namely, [the perfection of] giving corresponds to the hungry ghosts, ethical discipline to the hells, patience to animals, diligence to asuras, meditation to humans, and wisdom to devas.
The body of merit for the marks, cultivated over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* (and one hundred *kalpas*), is "fat" (*pīna*); this is likened to a fat sheep without fat.
The three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and so forth are correlated with the stages of the Śrāvaka.

The reason why Śrāvakas realize [enlightenment] swiftly while Bodhisattvas require the passage of kalpas is that, beneath the Buddha-tree, they exhaust both the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and their active manifestations (*paryavasthāna*). This is the interpretation of the meaning;
Śākyamuni thus transcended nine kalpas [of practice]. (Entrustment/Record) Quoting the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Maitreya should possess the transcendence of kalpas (the prediction); the Sanskrit text has not yet reached this point.

In the commentary on the lower section of the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Tongjiao), the three baskets (*piṭaka*) refute the practice of giving (*dāna*), while the common teaching refutes the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The practice of the Bodhisattva’s severing of fetters (*saṃyojana*) is common [to both].

The Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of the Shared Teaching exhaust both the two types of residual habits at the stage of Buddhahood— having severed the primary afflictions and diminished the residual habits—
and yet they vow to sustain the appearance of these residual habits arising for the sake of benefiting others.

The Separate Teaching, Lower (Appendix Note): The distinctness of each stage, both preceding and succeeding; (and) the Perfect [Teaching] has not yet distinguished the subsequent stages, thus they are not called "unshared.
In the various stages of the Separate Teaching, the characteristics of subduing and severing are distinct; turning toward the Perfect [Teaching], one cultivates the Perfect and severs [delusions].
This is illustrated by the analogy of separately smelting iron versus the analogy of burning gold.

The Separate Teaching (biejiao) clarifies the provisional nature of phenomena in contrast to the real; it elucidates the characteristics of the "lower" perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*),

using the metaphors of reflections in a mirror and the moon in water to illustrate the cultivation of the three thousand realms within both the phenomenal (*xiu*) and the noumenal (*xing*), as well as the severance of delusions within the perfect stages (*yuanwei*).
The Buddha knows and the Buddha sees; possessing the three knowledges and the five eyes, he is designated as "Buddha" by virtue of his excellence.

The principle that wisdom and substance are a non-dual unity is like the metaphor of the left and right hands;

This is the third section of the *Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning). In this chapter, the central tenet is that of resonance and response (*ganying*).

While other sutras take cause and effect as their primary tenet— such as the *Kauśalya-sūtra* which focuses on extracting suffering and the *Kauśalya-sūtra* which focuses on bestowing peace and joy— this chapter is not like them;
rather, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* clarify the causes and effects of Avalokiteśvara.
